propositions.text: The principal claimant and her husband are Chinese citizens claiming refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: XXXX XXX XX, the principal claimant, (hereinafter referred to as "the claimant") and her husband, XXXX XXXX XXXX, the male claimant, are citizens of the People's Republic of China (China). They claim refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimants are Chinese citizens seeking refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).

propositions.text: Claimants introduced to Christianity in 2007 and attended house church regularly
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2007, the claimants were introduced to Christianity and started attending a house church on XXXX, 2007. They continued to attend the services on a regular basis.

propositions.text: PSB approached house church in 2008; claimants escaped and hid
propositions.quote: While attending a service on XXXX, 2008, the members of the house church were informed by one of the lookouts that the Public Security Bureau (PSB) were approaching the house. The claimants managed to escape and immediately went to a relative's home where they stayed in hiding until their departure from China.

propositions.text: PSB visited claimants' home looking for them; claimants left China with smuggler in 2008
propositions.quote: During this time, the claimants came to know that the PSB had been to their home looking for them. With the assistance of a smuggler, the claimants left China and traveled to Canada on XXXX, 2008.

propositions.text: Claimants made refugee claim in Canada in 2008; female claimant gave birth to second daughter; first daughter remains in China
propositions.quote: They made a claim for refugee protection on XXXX, 2008. Subsequent to their arrival in Canada, the female claimant became pregnant and gave birth to a second daughter. Their first daughter is in China.

propositions.text: Claimants fear forced sterilization or imprisonment if returned to China due to second child
propositions.quote: The claimants also fear, if they return to China, they will be sterilized or imprisoned because of the birth of their second child.

paragraphs.summary: The claimants were introduced to Christianity in 2007, attended house church, escaped PSB raid in 2008, fled China, claimed refugee status in Canada, and fear sterilization if returned, says earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Credibility of claimants' testimony and PIF narratives about Christian identity and PSB pursuit is determinative
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in regard to this claim is the credibility of the claimants' oral testimony and Personal Information Form (PIF) narratives concerning their Christian identities and their pursuit by the authorities in China.

propositions.text: Claimants are not credible witnesses on Christian identity and PSB pursuit on balance of probabilities
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants are not credible witnesses in this regard.

propositions.text: Claimant revealed pregnancy at first sitting; claimants fear forced sterilization or imprisonment due to second child
propositions.quote: At the end of the first sitting, when making their submissions, the claimant revealed she was pregnant. During the second sitting, the claimants alleged that they cannot return to China because they fear forced sterilization or imprisonment because they gave birth to a second child, contrary to China's Family Planning Policy.

propositions.text: Relationship of subjective fear to objective situation of forced sterilization or imprisonment in Guangdong is determinative
propositions.quote: The determinative issue with respect to this part of the claim is the relationship of the claimants' subjective fear of persecution to the objective situation of forced sterilization or imprisonment in their home province of Guangdong, China.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds credibility of claimants' Christian identity and PSB pursuit testimony is key and finds them not credible; also considers their fear of sterilization in Guangdong.

propositions.text: Claimants are not Convention refugees as they lack well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in China
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimants are not Convention refugees as they do not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in China.

propositions.text: Claimants are not persons in need of protection; removal to China poses no personal risk to life, cruel treatment, or torture
propositions.quote: The panel also finds that the claimants are not persons in need of protection in that their removal to China would not subject them personally to a risk to their lives or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and in that there are no substantial grounds to believe that their removal to China will subject them personally to a danger of torture.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons needing protection as removal to China poses no personal risk.

propositions.text: Claimants established personal and Chinese national identities through testimony and documents
propositions.quote: The claimants established their personal identities and their identities as nationals of China through their testimony and the documents they presented.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimants established their personal and Chinese national identities through testimony and documents.

propositions.text: Claimants did not attend a house church in China as alleged, on balance of probabilities
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants did not attend a house church in China as they allege.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimants likely did not attend a house church in China as they allege.

propositions.text: Negative inference drawn from claimant's inconsistent evidence about house church service days
propositions.quote: The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility due to her inconsistent evidence concerning the house church services.

paragraphs.summary: The panel draws a negative inference on claimant's credibility due to inconsistent evidence about house church service days.

propositions.text: Claimant's testimony about days of house church services is inconsistent and explanation unsatisfactory
propositions.quote: With respect to the days of the week the house church services were held, the claimant testified that there were no specific days of the week. However, the claimant's PIF provides that the house church services "were always held on Sundays". When the claimant was asked about this inconsistent evidence, she stated that the services were mostly held on Sundays, but they also took place on Saturdays. The panel is not satisfied by the claimant's explanation as it does not account for the inconsistency between her oral evidence and her PIF narrative. Moreover, it provides a further inconsistency as she had earlier testified that the services were not held on any particular day of the week. The panel draws a further negative inference with respect to the claimant's shifting evidence in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's inconsistent testimony about house church service days unsatisfactory and draws further negative inference.

propositions.text: Claimant's testimony about times of house church services is inconsistent and explanation unsatisfactory
propositions.quote: With respect to the times the house church services were held, the claimant testified that the services were held at 7:30 to 9:00 in the evening. Yet, in her PIF, the claimant stated that the services were "always" held from 7:00 to 8:30pm. When the claimant was asked about this inconsistency, she stated that the services were not exactly on time all the time and usually they would gather around 7:00pm and once everyone arrived they would start, adding that the time was not exact. The panel is not satisfied by the claimant's shifting testimony to account for the inconsistency and draws a further negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's inconsistent testimony about house church service times unsatisfactory and draws further negative inference.

propositions.text: Claimant gave inconsistent evidence about baptisms, including timing and location
propositions.quote: The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility due to her inconsistent evidence concerning the claimants' baptisms. The panel asked the claimant whether she was baptized in her house church in China. She replied: "No". She was asked if her husband was baptized in their house church in China. Again, she replied: "No". The claimant explained that she and her husband planned to be baptized in China on XXXX 2008, as is indicated in their PIFs. The claimant went on to testify that she and her husband were baptized on XXXX 2007. She also stated that she had been attending the house church for one year before being baptized. However, the panel noted that she would have been attending the house church for days before being baptized, since she stated that she started attending the house church on XXXX, 2007. The claimant hesitated before replying that the baptisms took place on XXXX 2008 and it was by the sprinkling of water. She was asked when XXXX was celebrated in 2008. She stated in XXXX. The panel noted that XXXX was celebrated in XXXX of 2008. Given the significance of baptism to Christians, it is reasonable for the claimant to have recalled the correct month of her alleged baptism, less than two years earlier. The claimant's evidence then shifted, saying that she was not baptized in China at all. She then went on to say that she was not baptized on XXXX 2008, but rather on that occasion she witnessed other people's baptisms. The claimant was given the opportunity to explain why her previous oral evidence provided that she was baptized on XXXX 2008 by the sprinkling of water. She said she saw other people being baptized. The panel is not satisfied by the claimant's shifting evidence in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant gave inconsistent and shifting evidence about baptisms, undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant gave inconsistent evidence about distance of PSB at raid; explanation unsatisfactory
propositions.quote: The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility as a result of her inconsistent evidence concerning the time she says she saw the PSB at the time of the raid. The claimant testified that the PSB were about 50 metres away when she saw them the night her house church was raided. However, according to the Record of Examination3 (RoE), when the claimant was interviewed by an Immigration Officer (IO), she informed the IO that the PSB were 30 metres away when she saw them that evening. The claimant was asked to clarify her evidence in this regard. She stated that she is not very good with distance, like 30 or 50 metres, it could be any distance. The panel is not satisfied by the claimant's explanation. It is not reasonable for the claimant to have provided this explanation only subsequent to the panel noting the discrepancy in her RoE.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's inconsistent evidence about PSB distance at raid and unsatisfactory explanation undermine credibility.

propositions.text: Claimants are not being pursued by PSB as alleged, based on negative inferences and findings
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on the basis of the negative inferences and findings noted above and below, that the claimants are not being pursued by the PSB as they allege.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimants are not being pursued by PSB as they allege, based on negative inferences.

propositions.text: Claimant gave inconsistent evidence about dates and timing of PSB visits to home; explanation unsatisfactory
propositions.quote: The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility due to her inconsistent evidence concerning the times the PSB went to their home looking for the claimants. The claimant testified that the PSB went to her home on XXXX, 2008 in their pursuit of the claimants. She was asked how long she had been in Canada when the PSB went to her home this time. She stated about one week. The panel noted that the male claimant whispered something to his wife at that point in the hearing and he was reminded to refrain from making any comments or statements and he would be given the opportunity to say whatever he wanted to later. The panel also noted that the claimants say they arrived in Canada on XXXX, 2008 and, therefore, this visit would have taken place 17 days after she arrived in Canada. The claimant stated that maybe she made a mistake listening. The claimant was asked how she is able to remember the specific date of XXXX, 2008, as the time the PSB went to her home again. She said because at that time her mother telephoned her. Later in the hearing, the claimant stated that the second time the PSB went to her home was on XXXX, 2008, not XXXX. In any case, the panel noted that the claimants do not refer to this PSB visit in their PIFs. In fact, the only visits the claimants refer to occurred on XXXX, 2008 and XXXX, 2008. When given the opportunity to explain this inconsistency, she replied that the visit would have been around that time. The panel is not satisfied by the explanation as it does not account for the inconsistency. Moreover, the claimant put the second PSB visit in a context by saying that she remembered the date of the visit as it was at that time her mother telephoned her. Also given the significance of this visit with respect to the PSB's alleged pursuit of the claimants, it is reasonable for their evidence in this regard to be more consistent.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's inconsistent evidence about PSB visits to home and unsatisfactory explanation undermine credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant gave inconsistent evidence about PSB's reason for visit; explanation unsatisfactory
propositions.quote: The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility due to her inconsistent evidence surrounding the PSB's visit to their home. The claimant testified that the PSB went to her home looking for her. When asked why the PSB went to her home, she replied that she did not know. She testified that the PSB told her mother to tell her and her husband to report themselves to them, but she did not know why she had to report to them. She reiterated again that she did not know why she was asked to report to the PSB. She was asked if the PSB said or did anything else. She replied in the negative. However, in their PIFs, the claimants provide: "The police told my mother that we must report immediately to the PSB because we had attended an illegal church." The claimant was given the opportunity to explain her inconsistent evidence in this regard. She stated that her mother told her about the PSB having gone to their home and it was her conclusion that it was because she and her husband had joined the house church. The panel is not satisfied by the claimant's shifting evidence in this regard. Her PIF clearly provides that the PSB informed her mother of the reason why the claimants were to report themselves to their office.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's inconsistent evidence about PSB's reason for visit and unsatisfactory explanation undermine credibility.

propositions.text: No summons was shown or left despite PSB visits; panel questions PSB's genuine interest
propositions.quote: The claimants also says that despite this, no summons was ever shown to their family or left for them. The panel cannot help but question the genuine interest of the PSB in the claimants.

propositions.text: County document evidence shows police commonly leave summons with family when seeking someone
propositions.quote: County document evidence4 indicates that it is very common for police authorities to leave a summons or subpoena with family members when the police want someone to come to their headquarters.

propositions.text: Summons is basis for arrest warrant if person does not respond
propositions.quote: In addition, the summons is the documentary basis for the subsequent issuance of an arrest warrant if the person in whom they are interested does not respond to the summons.

propositions.text: Given PSB visits, reasonable to expect a summons would have been issued to claimants
propositions.quote: Although this policy is not always implemented, it is reasonable that one would have been issued in respect of the claimants given that the claimants testified that the PSB had gone to their home at least twice in search of them.

paragraphs.summary: The panel notes no summons was shown despite PSB visits, questions PSB's interest, and notes police commonly leave summons with family.

propositions.text: Claimant gave inconsistent evidence about how she learned of PSB visit; explanation unsatisfactory
propositions.quote: The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility due to her inconsistent evidence concerning how she came to know of the PSB's visit to her home in their alleged pursuit to them. The claimant testified that her mother telephoned her and informed her of the PSB's visit to her home. However, the claimants' PIF provides: "We heard from our friend that the police went to our home to try to arrest us." The claimant was given the opportunity to clarify her evidence in this regard. She stated that her mother telephoned her using her friend's telephone line and not from home. The panel is not satisfied by the claimant's unreasonable explanation. The PIF narrative provides that the claimants "heard from our friend" of the PSB's pursuit. The claimant's explanation that this means her mother called her using her friend's telephone is neither reasonable nor logical.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's inconsistent evidence about how she learned of PSB visit and unsatisfactory explanation undermine credibility.

propositions.text: Claimants were not genuine practicing Christians in China; credibility doubts arise
propositions.quote: On the basis of findings and negative inferences noted above concerning their alleged experiences in China, and, on a balance or probabilities, the panel finds that the claimants were not genuine practicing Christians in China, and that these credibility findings noted above concerning their China experience raise a significant doubt about their general credibility.

propositions.text: Claimants attend church and bible classes regularly in Canada and have adequate basic Christian knowledge
propositions.quote: The claimants stated that they attend church services regularly in Canada and have also attended bible classes. The claimants demonstrated an adequate knowledge of the basic tenets of Christianity.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimants were not genuine Christians in China, raising credibility doubts, but they attend church and have Christian knowledge in Canada.

propositions.text: Letter from pastor and baptismal certificate have little evidentiary weight on genuineness of faith
propositions.quote: The panel gives little evidentiary weight to these documents.

propositions.text: Claimant disclosed letter from pastor and baptismal certificate
propositions.quote: In addition, the claimant disclosed a letter from their pastor, Rev. XX of XXXX XXXX XXXX in Toronto and a baptismal certificate.

propositions.text: Pastor's assessment of faith genuineness cannot substitute panel's assessment
propositions.quote: case law6 indicates that a pastor's assessment of the genuineness of a person's faith cannot be substituted for the assessment that the panel is required to make.

propositions.text: Possession of Christian knowledge or documents does not necessarily reflect genuine Christian practice or motivation
propositions.quote: The mere possession of some knowledge of Christianity in itself is not necessarily a reflection of genuine Christian practice. Moreover, these documents can only attest to the claimant's participation in church activities, they do not attest to her motivation.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds pastor's letter and baptismal certificate have little weight; pastor's view cannot replace panel's assessment of faith genuineness.

propositions.text: Difficult to judge genuineness of religious practice; claimants not genuine Christians in China or Canada
propositions.quote: It is difficult to make a judgement regarding the genuineness of a person's religious practice. However, on the basis of findings and negative inferences noted above concerning their alleged experiences in China, and on a balance or probabilities, the panel finds that the claimants were not genuine practicing Christians in China, and that these credibility findings noted above concerning their China experience raise a significant doubt about her general credibility. Having found that the claimants were not practicing Christians in China, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of findings noted above, that the claimants were not Christians when they arrived in Canada, and whatever knowledge of Christianity the claimants now possess was obtained in Toronto and only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim. In this context, and on the basis of the totality of evidence disclosed, the panel therefore finds that the claimants are not now genuine practicing Christians.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimants were not genuine Christians in China or Canada; knowledge gained in Toronto to support fraudulent claim.

propositions.text: Claimants first disclosed pregnancy and fear of forced sterilization at end of first sitting
propositions.quote: It was only when making their submissions at the end of the first sitting did the claimants inform the panel, for the first time, that the female claimant is pregnant and they fear return to China because they have breached family planning policy.

propositions.text: Claimants fear sterilization or imprisonment due to second child
propositions.quote: The claimants further explained that they fear being sterilized or imprisoned because they had a second child.

propositions.text: Claimants' subjective fear of forced sterilization or imprisonment not supported by objective situation in Guangdong
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants' subjective fear of forced sterilization or imprisonment is not supported by the objective situation in Guangdong province.

paragraphs.summary: The panel notes claimants first disclosed pregnancy and fear of sterilization late; finds subjective fear unsupported by objective Guangdong situation.

propositions.text: In Guangdong Province, parents with one more child than permitted are charged a social support fee, not sterilization or imprisonment.
propositions.quote: In Guangdong Province, the claimant's home province, the preponderance of the evidence indicates that where there is one more child than permitted, the parents will be charged a social support fee.

propositions.text: Guangdong Family Planning Regulations, 2002 impose fines for out of plan births, increasing for second births.
propositions.quote: The Guangdong Family Planning Regulations, 2002, stipulates that a social compensation fine is imposed for out of plan births. This document not only noted a fine for the first additional child but additional and enhanced fines for the second out of plan births.

propositions.text: No reports of forced sterilization in Guangdong province found in IRB Research Directorate sources for 2002-2005.
propositions.quote: In addition, no reports of specific incidents of forced sterilization in the Guangdong province, the claimant's home province, could be found among sources consulted by the Research Directorate of the IRB for the period 2002-2005.

propositions.text: Recent government decisions in Guangdong focus on charging social fees for out of plan births rather than forced sterilization or imprisonment.
propositions.quote: it is clear that the thrust of recent decisions by the Government of China and in particular by Guangdong provincial officials, the claimant's home province is toward charging a social fee for out of plan births.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Guangdong charges social fees for extra children, no forced sterilization reports, and recent policies favor fines over sterilization or imprisonment.

propositions.text: Country documents report scarce information on forced sterilization of men in China.
propositions.quote: Country documents also provide that information on the forced sterilization of men in China was reported to be "scarce".

propositions.text: Sterilization rates among women in China are significantly higher than for men.
propositions.quote: One report indicated that sterilization rates among women in China are "significantly" higher than for males.

paragraphs.summary: Country documents show forced sterilization of men is scarce and women's sterilization rates are significantly higher.

propositions.text: UNFPA representative said provincial family planning regulations enacted in 2002 or after have legal status.
propositions.quote: the representative for the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) in China commented that, while provincial family planning regulations prior to 2002 were considered to be administrative guidelines, provincial regulations enacted in 2002 or after have the status of law

propositions.text: UNFPA analyses indicate provincial regulations are becoming flexible and more aligned with international standards.
propositions.quote: the organization's analyses of trends in population and family planning policies in China would indicate that provincial regulations are becoming "flexible" and "their implementation is equally getting progressively more in line with international standards".

paragraphs.summary: UNFPA says post-2002 provincial family planning laws are legally binding and becoming more flexible and aligned with international standards.

propositions.text: UNFPA informed that local Family Planning officials are evaluated on quality of care, not birth quotas.
propositions.quote: local Family Planning officials are no longer being evaluated by government officials on the basis of meeting birth quotas, but rather on the quality of care being provided.

paragraphs.summary: UNFPA states local family planning officials are evaluated on quality of care, not birth quotas.

propositions.text: China and Guangdong Province recognize social responsibility to change birth control policies, addressing gender imbalance.
propositions.quote: there is also evidence that the Government of China and its constituent provincial authorities, especially Guangdong Province, have recognised a pragmatic as well as a social responsibility to change their birth control policies. In this regard, the gender imbalance has become an important issue of concern.

propositions.text: No reports of forced sterilizations in Guangdong province found in IRB Research Directorate sources.
propositions.quote: In regard to specific incidents of forced sterilizations in Guangdong province, the claimants' home province, none could be found in reports from sources consulted by the IRB Research Directorate.

propositions.text: Rural couples are given more flexibility regarding a second child in China.
propositions.quote: country documents indicate that rural couples are given more flexibility regarding a second child.

propositions.text: Current trend is to impose fines; forced sterilization or imprisonment is not probable for out of plan births.
propositions.quote: it appears to be clear that the current trend is to impose fines and forced sterilization or imprisonment is not a probable result of the birth of an out of plan child.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds China and Guangdong address gender imbalance, no forced sterilization reports, rural couples get flexibility, fines likely over sterilization or imprisonment.

propositions.text: Country documents cite media reports on China's concern about gender imbalance and rewards for couples with daughters.
propositions.quote: country documents cite media reports in regard to China's concern about the growing gender imbalance and efforts made to reward couples with daughters.

propositions.text: Claimant likely allowed a second child given time lapse and Guangdong's gender disparity.
propositions.quote: it is more likely than not that the claimant, whose first daughter was born in China on XXXX, 2000, would be allowed to have a second child, also considering the extended lapse of time since the birth of the claimants' daughter, especially in Guangdong, the claimant's home province, which has a particularly high disparity between the number of newborn girls and boys.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant likely allowed second child due to gender imbalance concerns and time since first child's birth.

propositions.text: Persons with unauthorized children born abroad likely face no penalties upon return to China.
propositions.quote: The preponderance of the evidence indicates that it is more likely than not that a person who has an unauthorized child while living abroad would not face penalties upon returning to China.

propositions.text: People returning to China from abroad are welcomed and children born outside are largely forgiven.
propositions.quote: people who return to China from abroad are actively welcomed back to the 'motherland,' and children born outside China largely forgiven.

propositions.text: Document does not exclude mothers or couples who left China illegally from forgiveness.
propositions.quote: The document does not provide that it excludes mothers or couples who left China illegally.

propositions.text: University of Alberta professor noted Chinese nationals with children abroad may not be subject to one-child policy.
propositions.quote: an associate professor and Mactaggart Research Chair of the China Institute at the University of Alberta likewise noted that Chinese nationals who have children while abroad may not be subject to the one-child policy.

propositions.text: Country documents cite media reports on China's concern about gender imbalance and rewards for couples with daughters.
propositions.quote: country documents cite media reports in regard to China's concern about the growing gender imbalance and efforts made to reward couples with daughters.

propositions.text: Claimants have one daughter born in China in 2000 and a second daughter born in Canada in 2010.
propositions.quote: The claimants have one daughter in China, born in XXXX, 2000. Their second child born in Canada ten years later, on XXXX, 2010, is also a daughter.

propositions.text: Claimants' second child likely welcomed back to China.
propositions.quote: it is more likely than not that the claimants' child would be welcomed back to China.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds unauthorized children born abroad likely face no penalties on return; claimants' second child likely welcomed back.

propositions.text: Country documents indicate children born outside China with foreign citizenship are not counted by family planning officials.
propositions.quote: country documents indicate that a child born out of China, who acquires foreign citizenship, is not included in counts by family planning officials.

propositions.text: Claimant's child born in Canada will not be included in family planning counts on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's child born in Canada will not be included in counts by family planning officials.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant's Canadian-born child with foreign citizenship will not be counted by family planning officials.

propositions.text: News sources report an emerging class of rich Chinese citizens pay fines or travel overseas for additional children.
propositions.quote: country document evidence cites news sources that report that there is an emerging class of rich Chinese citizens who simply pay a fine or travel overseas to have additional children.

paragraphs.summary: News reports show rich Chinese pay fines or go abroad for additional children.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence that persons breaching family planning policy face imprisonment.
propositions.quote: there is no persuasive evidence before the panel that persons who have breached China's family planning policy would face imprisonment.

propositions.text: Claimants given opportunity to explain risk of imprisonment or sterilization.
propositions.quote: The panel gave the claimants the opportunity to explain why they think they will be imprisoned or sterilized.

propositions.text: Claimant testified a friend was sterilized.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that a friend of hers was sterilized.

propositions.text: Claimant's friend's circumstances differ from claimants; friend had two children in China, so testimony given little weight.
propositions.quote: the panel notes that the claimant's description of this friend's personal circumstances is very different from that of the claimants: This friend gave birth to a daughter and then a son. Moreover, this friend also gave birth to her two children in China. Therefore, the panel gives the claimant's testimony with respect to this friend little weight.

paragraphs.summary: No evidence supports imprisonment risk; claimant's sterilized friend testimony given little weight due to differing circumstances.

propositions.text: Mixed messages exist on government policy for out of plan births, but evidence favors fines over sterilization or imprisonment.
propositions.quote: there are clearly mixed messages concerning government policy and action concerning out of plan births. However, on the basis of the totality of the evidence available to the panel in regard to this claim, the panel is persuaded by the document cited above. The panel finds that the preponderant message from both Chinese government sources and independent sources is that an enhanced fine rather than forced sterilization or imprisonment is more likely than not the penalty that would be faced by the claimants.

paragraphs.summary: Despite mixed messages, evidence shows fines more likely than sterilization or imprisonment for out of plan births.

propositions.text: Gender Guidelines do not mitigate findings that fines are more likely than forced sterilization or imprisonment.
propositions.quote: The panel has also given serious consideration to the Gender Guidelines. The panel finds no constraint in this regard that should mitigate the findings noted above.

paragraphs.summary: Gender Guidelines do not alter the finding that fines are more likely than sterilization or imprisonment.

propositions.text: Claimants' subjective fear of persecution not supported by objective situation in Guangdong province.
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants' subjective fear of persecution is not supported by the objective situation in Guangdong province.

propositions.text: Claimants are not at risk of forced sterilization or imprisonment by Family Planning officials.
propositions.quote: The panel further finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants are not at risk of forced sterilization and imprisonment by Family Planning officials.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimants' fear unsupported and no risk of forced sterilization or imprisonment.

propositions.text: Male claimant agrees with wife's evidence; his claim relies on her evidence and fails for lack of differentiation.
propositions.quote: the male claimant testified that he agreed with the oral evidence provided by his wife. As the claims of the male claimant rely almost entirely on the evidence of the claimant and no persuasive evidence was adduced to differentiate her claims from his, his claim must also fail.

paragraphs.summary: Male claimant's claim fails as it relies on wife's evidence without differentiation.

propositions.text: Claimants have not established serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment or torture in China.
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimants have not satisfied their burden of establishing a serious possibility that they would be persecuted or that they would be personally subjected to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants fail to show serious possibility of persecution or cruel treatment risk in China.

propositions.text: Considering all protection grounds, no serious possibility of persecution or risk to life, cruel treatment, or torture found.
propositions.quote: The panel has considered all three protection grounds under s. 96 and ss. 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and, on the basis of the totality of all the evidence made available to the panel, finds that there is not a serious possibility that the claimants would be persecuted in China, nor that they would be subjected personally to a risk to their lives, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds no serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment or torture under protection grounds.

propositions.text: Claims are rejected for reasons stated.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the claims are rejected.

paragraphs.summary: Claims are rejected by the panel.
